Oh, it's a pleasure. And Jacob, tell us a little bit about yourself.
And also, for those who haven't heard of Legora, tell us a little bit about what

So yeah, my name is Jacob. I'm the CTO at Legora.

Legora is a sort of workspace product platform for legal

That's amazing. And yeah, like, you know, a lot of people who maybe haven't

So it's great to hear that perspective. One thing for those who haven't heard is
that you've hit 100 million ARR across 18 months.
Is that around correct? I didn't misquote there?
No, you're right. It took us 18 months to get to 100 million.
And last week we just announced 200 million.
And that took us six months.
Wow. Congratulations. It's amazing when companies do this.
What does it look like from the perspective of the head of engineering,
the CTO?
I mean, I think it's just always exciting that people get value from the product

That's sort of the thing for us, right? And then, you know, you can imagine a

We have so much usage now. But it's super exciting.
I mean, everyone is super thrilled.
Amazing. And let's look a little bit under the covers, because obviously that kind of
speed of growth from a company requires huge flexibility and speed from the point
of view of the engineering team, the company underneath.
And I'd love to jump into some of the AI practices that you use.
From what I understand, AI writes over half of Legora's codebase, and I hear...
I think
all of it.
Pretty much all of it. Wow.
Yeah yeah yeah yeah.
Now, I heard some engineers can run ten concurrent agents at the same
time. First of all, I'd love to understand how quickly did your team get to such a
level? Because, you know, I've played with two or three, and it does take time to

And then secondly, I'd love to hear maybe some of the pain points along the way.
What were some of the problems or, dare I say, outages maybe that these kind of
practices caused?
Yeah.
First question, how quickly did people get here?
That's very quickly. I think we've always hired for people that are extremely
forward leaning and people that
challenge themselves all the time. And when you have that type of talent pool,
they'll adopt technology really quickly.
Going from a few agents to a lot of agents
was also relatively quick.
There was a lot of tooling. I think you asked about pain points.
That was definitely one of them, building the tools that let us orchestrate many
agents. We built a custom background sort of coding agent that we could launch.
We invested into cloud dev setups so that one agent can have its own cloud setup and
run its own, you know, logs and observability and everything, and send
back videos and screenshots of what it's working on.
But also our own... I mean, there's a few engineers that are sharing a tool that
they built, which is like a Kanban board for agents, and that's one way to

Another one is we spent some time figuring out how we could have multiple

dev.
So, for example, you know, our app requires spinning up Postgres and Redis

etc. And then we built this custom tool that allows us to have one instance of all
of those running and then share them across all of our workspaces.
So all agents have their own, you know, database in Postgres, their own prefix in
Redis, whatever it is, so that we can use the resources on our local laptops
efficiently.
Nice. And I presume the parallelization here is happening across not just a single
feature or piece of work, like maybe you would on a worktree, but
you're having individual developers running multiple pieces of functionality
and running different tickets at the same time.
Yeah, absolutely. And that's just the developers that are working on their
features or whatever they're building now.
But we have full loops that don't even involve developers or developers' machines
themselves, right? We have our bug reporting Slack channel.
When there's a bug that comes in, it kicks off a cloud agent that tries to reproduce
it, and if it can reproduce it, it sends video evidence back into Slack.
And then it fixes it and writes a regression test and opens a PR, and then
an engineer, a goalie, will take a look and review and get that merged.
So we have whole sort of loops and work that runs outside of any actual engineer.
Yeah. I'd love to also double down on one thing that you mentioned, which is the
types of engineers that you hire. You know, they absolutely
need to be forward AI thinking. When we think about senior developers who
are, I guess, what we would call old school senior developers, versus a
young... well, maybe I shouldn't say young...
a
more AI-first developer who hasn't been, let's say, tainted
by the more traditional styles of software development, do you have an inkling as to
which you would almost prefer, or which you see the better results from?
I think
generally people that are very fast learners, that's strictly a good thing.
So people that are very curious and super ambitious to learn and try new things,
that's the type of people we hire for, regardless of age or background.
Then
there's definitely some advantages to being very senior and having seen a lot of
stuff, especially when it comes to really big scale or distributed systems or
databases, where it's just very helpful to have seen some stuff.
But then it's all about finding those people that have seen a lot of stuff and
have a lot of experience, but are still extremely forward leaning.
There's a Venn diagram and some overlap there.
And those people, I find, if you have a lot of experience and you're a really good
engineer and architect, and you're then also super into AI and really good at
using agents, then you're a force to be reckoned with.
I think those engineers are just extremely valuable.
Yeah, it seems to me sometimes you have a lot of people that are experienced but
almost are held back by trying to do things the more traditional old way,
versus trying to fix problems that may not even exist in today's world.
And I even heard someone say that you could comfortably substitute some of that
experience for someone who is hungry and ready to essentially prioritize speed.
Yeah. I think it really comes down to the person, right?
I think both are super valuable. I think speed is extremely important.
So solving tomorrow's problem is really important.
But I think some part of systems thinking and thinking six months ahead is also
really, really important. If you can look around corners, it's really important,
especially as you scale the team.
I think if you're a small team of ten engineers, then the only thing that
matters is tomorrow. Like, you just have to fight for survival at that point.
But if you're a hundred engineers and everyone has that mindset where it's only
about tomorrow, then you're going to end up with a codebase that's completely
unmanageable, and you're going to have a lot of incidents, and you can't really
scale that very well. Whereas if you have a few more systems thinkers, you can
actually build a system where you can have a lot of people running on it, and you can
get a lot of gains from the technical investments that you're making.
So I guess also, Jacob, from the point of view of
someone in a senior position as part of an engineering organization, it's really
important to be able to know
how much your organization has adopted AI.
Now, you've criticized token maxing as a way of measuring that adoption of AI.
First of all, talk us through that a little bit.
Yeah, I think there was probably an era, maybe at its
peak six months ago, where everyone was talking about token maxing, and people had
leaderboards of how many tokens people are using, and leaders would track them and
they would tell people, you're not using enough tokens.
And some people would even build this into their career ladder.
Like, the more tokens you use, the better it is.
I didn't do this ever, but I talked to other people in the industry and they, you
know, just have engineers that would just burn tokens to burn tokens, right?
They just have them running in loops, doing nothing.
Obviously that's not the right solution. And so I think it's always been a really
bad way to encourage AI adoption, by telling people that they need to use a lot
of tokens. And I think instead it's way more important to focus on
just setting a high expectation for output and what we could get done.
And then you drive AI adoption through that, as a means to get more amazing work
done faster. And, you know, highlight all the wins and do some hackathons where
people show how you can work now, and open up people's eyes a little bit, I think.
Yeah, that's how I think about it. I think the industry is also coming around to the
idea that token maxing doesn't make any sense, and it's more about setting high
expectations.
Yeah. It feels like the new lines of code,
you know.
Exactly. That's exactly what it is.
Yeah. And when I do hear people say, oh yeah, if you're not token maxing, you're
not getting the most out of AI, most of the time they come from a frontier lab.
And obviously it's in their best interest to say that.
Yeah.
So what's on your dashboard at Legora to understand whether you are, you know,
adopting AI technologies?
Let's see. I'm not
the biggest proponent of trying to measure everything.
The thing that's most important to me is: are the teams delivering great stuff
really quickly? At the end of the day, that's what I care about.
Is the stuff that we're building great? Are our products great?
Is the architecture great? And are we doing it fast?
And honestly, if a team did it without using AI at all, that's great.
I don't actually really care. But I don't think that's possible.
I think
AI is an extremely powerful lever to get to that result.
So I mostly care about the result, and that's what I'm measuring on.
Is the design great or sloppy when we review the system with staff engineers and
architects, etc.? Does it make sense? And are we delivering projects really fast?
Then we have a developer experience team, a developer platform team, that's looking
a lot more at AI usage, to just make it very efficient.
And so we're looking at things like, okay, how many turns does it take us to get to
the place where we want to be?
How have we architected our system and our engine to produce code with agents in a

system and how we want the system to evolve?
That's a powerful
platform for all of our engineers. So that's something that I think a lot about:
how can we invest in the right things as an organization such that all engineers
are 5%, 10% more effective?
I think for many years that's been what a lot of leaders have thought about.
But now it's actually really possible, because you actually have this sort of one
knob that you can really invest into, which is AI enablement and AI guardrails
and whatever it is you set up, that actually has a really meaningful, very
quick impact on the engineering work that happens.
Yeah. And I guess there's AI assistance, AI enablement.
And when we talk about the autonomy of AI and the ability for it to actually replace
tasks or
pieces of work that
we would maybe find less interesting or time consuming, what's your belief on
how ready agents and AI models are
to actually start replacing pieces of human work?
What have you done in that space at Legora?
So I think if I look at this from our product, in legal,
AI can do all of the menial work. All of the stuff like looking through a million
documents to find red flags, and analyzing huge contracts against various laws, and
doing the legal research that's extremely time consuming and actually very difficult
to do. AI can do all of that now. And so it takes away all the menial, low value
tasks that lawyers used to be doing all the time, and they can focus on the high
value judgment and strategic work, which is really why people became lawyers.
You know, no one became a lawyer to sit and look through a million huge documents.
No one's excited about that.
Whether and how we take that
further:
I absolutely believe we can do that. But there's some parts that will always
require human judgment, or at least for the next ten years, say.
So let's think about it in terms of verification, right?
Certain tasks you can verify, and that's typically the tasks that AI will be really
good at. So that could be math, coding. You can get AI to do something and very
quickly check if it's correct. With coding, you can run tests.
That's the way to do code verification. You see a lot of people now that are
optimizing towards a single measure because it's verifiable, and AI is really
good at it. I'm sure that you've read a bunch of blog posts of lots of people
doing certain things. I mean, the Bun rewrite is a great example of this, where
there was a really big, really good test suite, which meant that they could do this
huge thing, because they could test it and they would know if it worked.
With legal, that's pretty difficult, because a lot of the tasks aren't
verifiable, and a lot of them also require a sort of strategic thinking and human

And I think that's one of the tests: if
there's no objective truth, then AI won't be able to do it.
It will still be able to
give you extreme amounts of value, but it can't do it autonomously, basically.
So there's a limit to certain things. And then I think our job is: how do we make
an interface or a product where
it's extremely efficient to bring your judgment into the system, and then agents

Interesting. And I think, obviously here, from a legal case, the ramifications of
getting something right or wrong are night and day.
I guess this brings me to another
very recent, very recent at the time of recording, tool, which is a
decision-making model like Jev. And we've actually done a lot of playing with this
ourselves and
I'm sure you have as well.
LLMs, yeah, they could be good at that kind of decision making.
However a
model like Jev, where it provides you with an answer one way or another with a

the workflow potentially, and then shares back to us as humans when confidence

we model our agents, our applications and workflows?
Yeah, I think that's absolutely possible.
It's almost weird to me now that decision models, even the early ones, or whatever
versions you had of this before, weren't much bigger.
Looking back, it's so obvious that a lot of AI stuff today, a lot of applied AI, is

And obviously you need them when you need to do writing or drafting or whatever it
is.
But no, it's something that's very top of mind for me: how can we use this?
How can we decompose our tasks? We're already really good at doing this, and

We haven't yet found out if the confidence scores that you get from decision models
are trustworthy. I remember I used to do these big classification models with
classifier heads and BERT models, and generally the confidence scores weren't

So I don't know if I'll trust those scores too much.
I haven't looked at Jev specifically, at how much I trust those scores, but

And if they can be calibrated very well, or maybe we will fine tune one for our
domain that's well calibrated, then that's certainly a very powerful

Yeah. And I was actually talking with someone today in our AI engineering team

And so we were actually wondering, well, if it has structured output, there is a

But I presume this is still going to

But it's very interesting. We haven't run any tests locally here to compare that,
and I'm not sure if you have or if you've seen anything like that either.
No. Well, not
big enough that I feel comfortable sharing anything.
But we actually have a product where we're doing this exact thing.
This is like two years back, and it's still working really well, where we

confidence, here's how it works. And
that's just a decision model, right?
It's interesting, because structured output is actually something that isn't
new. It is a couple of years old, right, like you say.
So, humans. Let's talk a little bit about when we get humans involved, the meat bags

We talked about low confidence. I presume critical decisions as well, or critical
projects. So for example, a legal case where something really does need
verification. How do you decide when autonomy can really be left to the agents
to decide, and when humans need to be involved?
Yeah, this is a great question. I'm not sure if we've yet nailed it.
I don't know if we ever will.
There's obviously user preference, so we can't just make a universal truth.
There's some users that are maybe new in their journey with AI, and they want to
confirm everything. Just like us in Claude Code initially, when we had to say yes to
every
tool it wanted to run, we'd say yes, yes, yes.
And now there's auto mode, which I think all engineers basically run on, or maybe
even ran on YOLO mode before.
So I think we need to bring everyone along for the ride.
And so there's some user preference there, where maybe you want to review everything
initially, and then as you get more comfortable,
we can do more and more stuff autonomously.
And I really am working towards this future where it's more the
agent soliciting input from the human than the other way around.
And so I think we're moving towards having a lot more proactive agents that are
always on and always doing work, and then they will come and say, hey, I need some
input. You know, we found this red flag in this contract.
How do you want us to handle it? There are these two paths, or whatever it might be.
And
speaking about an interface for effective human judgment input, I think that's an
example of a really efficient way to provide human judgment.
Yeah. And I think it's one of those things that is a constantly moving goalpost as
well, as models change and as we adjust as well, and what users expect from the
product. It's a tough one to think. If you nail it, it might not be the same next
week, even if you...
Exactly. It changes every six months, basically, right?
Everyone feels more and more comfortable that AI does more and more.
And so, you know, maybe in two years no one's going to talk about this, because
we'll just always let it rip.
That's it. And it's funny how every single time, like, we talk about Jev being
released, and all of a sudden you get a new Luna.
Luna 6 comes out, and
in our tests it's a little bit slower than 5.6, but it's
half the price of 5.6. So you see these model vendors

It is. We're very excited about it, because I think in the past year it's been

Which makes sense, because they're trying to push AGI.
But I think for a lot of application companies like us, and loads of others
that I talk to that are in a similar situation, we're very excited about the

Not all tasks in coding or in legal or in finance require a country

And this is really interesting, because I know you benchmark ten plus models every

So are you using different models for different tasks?
Yeah yeah yeah.
And we do this in various different ways.
We decompose tasks into different sub-agents and subcomponents.
We have
different products that will use different models.
There's various ways that we decompose tasks and use different models.
And yeah, we change them per task, almost per week, depending on what's best.
Basically, part of our offering to our clients is that we
give them efficient AI,
easy to use,
abstracted away from them. They get the best of what exists, and we are really
experts at figuring that out.
And so to do that, we have to test these models all the time and always give them
what's Pareto efficient. And that's also why
law firms trust us and corporates trust us, because they know that not only do
they get great AI, which was the most important thing a year ago, but now great

So they essentially replay a whole bunch of the trickiest user questions there are.

Or are models not quite so varied these days?
No, it actually is. It's definitely something.
But it's not just models. We need these both for models but also for the harness

Yeah. Super interesting. I want to come back to something that you've said in the

when we think about the interactions. And we talked about Jev, which is now designed

And this kind of
leads us into an AI native interface, a place
whereby we expect
agents to take in very different inputs and provide very different outputs, maybe
for consumption by an agent rather than a human.
What does an AI native interface look like when we think about models, or how should
we think about it?
I think there's layers to this.
I'm pretty intrigued generally about the way that we're solving
intelligence via natural language. I mean, even in robotics,
a lot of robots are humanoids,
which I think is interesting, right? Because we're trying to create artificial
intelligence to look very much like human intelligence, or even look like humans and
act like humans. And maybe that's the right direction, but it seems inefficient
to me. It seems like maybe a necessary first step before we can actually move to
something that makes more sense. I think there's probably a physical build of a
robot that's way more efficient than looking like we do.
And the same thing for language models and for intelligence.
But that's sort of at the very high level.
I think if you look at a product like ours, the point that I was getting at back
then was that if you're doing really complex work, the most efficient
interface, going back to what I said before, for you to review that work and
understand that work and guide that work might not be a very long single chat
thread.
You know,
that's how I would collaborate with you if we were working on something together.
That would essentially be me talking to you, you talking to me, and there's a
bunch of messages back and forth. But
that's just the human constraint. This is the only way we have to communicate.
But people have communicated in other ways, right?
They've created slideshows or whatever.
And agents can do all this sort of stuff right off the bat.
So I think when you do a really big due diligence analysis now, analyzing millions
of documents, giving me the output of that huge analysis as a long chat message is
not super efficient. And so we've built a product which is essentially like a big

And that's a very efficient interface for me to review the work, because I can very
quickly go around and see what's actually happened.
And so I think that's an example of how we think about,
when we do really complex agent work, what's a good interface to interact with
that. And this is one example. There are more.
It's a
constantly moving target. I don't know what ends up being the right solution, but
I'm not convinced that everything is just going to be chat.
And I presume that extends to your context as well, in terms of your context doesn't
necessarily need to be human readable or in a form that's
consumable by us. It kind of makes me think the black box is turning even more
closed as well. And how do we actually understand if it's getting the right data?
We rely sometimes on verification or tests, but it's getting harder.
No, yeah, I think you're right. But I think that's also solvable in the same
system. That needs to be part of the system of interaction.
Part of the system of interaction needs to be auditability and understanding,
especially in our domain. If you're working on an extremely important case and

So right now we have multi-hop citations, basically, which is like, you click on

And no matter how we build our system, we need to ensure that it's auditable and
understandable and reliable by us as humans, so we know what's happened and can
say okay to this.
Yeah. And staying on context, actually, the way you talk about it, there is
obviously so much data, and there's very strong links and citations between various
documents and things like that. How complex a problem is context, and keeping
your context windows a reasonable size, making sure you have all the data?
Is this a significant pain when you have such a large volume of data to be
referencing?
Significant pain? I don't know. Everything represents
a significant pain.
Is it the most significant of your significant pains?
I don't think it's the most significant, but it's definitely up there.
I mean,
again, the goalpost keeps moving, right? Initially people were using Legora for
very simple things, and now they're using Legora for multiple hours.
They have agents that run for multiple hours and do extremely complex things.
And then this type of stuff is important, and we need to figure out how to solve
that. And we have different approaches and different methodologies to do that.
But yeah, it's a difficult thing to build an agent that can
work for the human equivalent of days. That's a difficult thing to do, and very
few people have solved that yet. And that's something that we continue to work
towards, and we're making really good progress.
I'm very excited to see what the future brings there.
Yeah, it's very interesting. And you once said, I think talking about context rot,
that the solution for context rot isn't to actually grow the context window bigger,
which sounds like it might be a reasonable thing.
Have you been burned by this
working through Legora, or is there a better path you've found?
You mean using models that have bigger context windows?
To solve the idea of stale context, context growing too quickly.
Yeah,
yeah. This is also a great question. Will we just get models that have a 100 million
token context window and then there's no problem at all?
Maybe. It doesn't look like that's the direction that things are going.
